1.x: “after six days”: the chronological marker is deliberate and mirrors the OT pattern of divine revelation. In Ex 24:16, the glory of the LORD(YHWH) settled on Mount Sinai, and the cloud covered it for SIX DAYS; on the seventh day, God called to Moses out of the cloud. Matthew’s timing signals that a major, Sinai-level revelation is about to occur. “Peter, James, and John his brother”: Jesus selects an inner circle from among the twelve apostles. By choosing exactly three witnesses, this gathering satisfies the legal requirement for establishing testimony under biblical law (“at the mouth of two witnesses, or at the mouth of three witnesses, shall the matter be established”, Deut 19:15). This specific trio is chosen to witness the peak of His glory here, just as they will later be chosen to witness the depth of His agony in the Garden of Gethsemane (Mt 26:37). “An high mountain apart”: mountains in Scripture are the traditional locations for divine encounters (Sinai, Horeb). This has a lot of symbolism in how we’re always to strive upwards, regardless of the difficulty of it, because we will not have a clear picture of what is next until we reach the top of the mountain & gain a better perspective.

2.x: Following immediately after Jesus’ declaration that some standing there would not taste death until they saw the Son of Man coming in his kingdom, Matthew records the fulfillment of that promise. This event (the Transfiguration) provides a physical, visionary unveiling of Christ’s royal and judicial glory. The glory was not a second person appearing nex to Jesus. Rather, the divine glory that normally remained veiled by the flesh became visible through the man Christ Jesus. The Transfiguration is a revelation of Christ's divine glory through his humanity. Hence: Jesus’s body/humanity is what the disciples physically saw; the shining glory is the deity dwelling in Him unveiled for a moment (the Father); the voice from heaven is God (the omnipresent Father) speaking from heaven as a sign for the disciples’ sake, see notes on v.5 (God is omnipresent, He can speak from wherever He’d like to). “God was IN Christ, reconciling the world unto Himself..” (2 Cor 5:19 KJV) - so the Transfiguration becomes a visible disclosure of that truth.

3.x: Moses represents the giving of the Law; Elijah represents the pinnacle of the Prophets. Their appearance alongside Jesus demonstrates that both the Law and the Prophets find their fulfillment, climax, and ultimate meaning in Jesus. Both figures had unusual departures from earthly life (Moses buried by God, Elijah caught up in a whirlwind) and both were expected to have roles preceding the Day of the LORD (Malachi 4:4-5 commands Israel to remember the Law of Moses and promises the return of Elijah before the “great and dreadful day”). Also, both Moses and Elijah had previously stood on Mount Sinai/Horeb to hear the voice of God in times of national crisis. Now, they stand on a new mountain to witness the Living Word. “talking with him”: Luke’s account adds that they were discussing His exodos (decease/departure) which he was about to accomplish at Jerusalem (Lk 9:31). The legal and prophetic foundations of Israel are shown to be completely aligned with Jesus’ looming sacrificial mission.

4.x: Peter proposes building three skenas (temporary shelters or booths), reminiscent of the Feast of Tabernacles (Sukkot).

5.x: The voice from heaven does not mean that God-the-Father is in heaven while God-the-Son is on earth. The voice from heaven is not for Jesus, it is for the disciple’s sake: “hear ye him.” Jesus did not need to hear: “this is my beloved Son,” he already knew that. But the disciples were going to go through some serious trials; Jesus needed to ensure their faith was strong enough to withstand it all. This is especially clear in John 12:28-30. Jesus says: “Father, glorify thy name.” Then a voice comes from heaven: “I have both glorified it, and will glorify it again.” Then Jesus immediately explains: “THIS VOICE CAME NOT BECAUSE OF ME, BUT FOR YOUR SAKES.” Jesus does not need reassurance from heaven, but the crowd needed divine confirmation of who Jesus was. The heavenly voice functioned as a sign for public testimony. So when God speaks from heaven at Jesus’ baptism or transfiguration, it is not because Jesus is having a conversation with another divine person for his own benefit, rather they are signs and revelatory speech directed towards the witnesses. Apply this same logic to Jesus’ baptism: “This is my beloved Son..” Who benefits from that statement? Not Jesus, he already knows his identity. Yet, it benefits John the Baptist, the crowd, and the later readers of the gospel. It publicly identifies Jesus as the Messiah. Likewise at the Transfiguration: “Hear ye him.” That phrase is addressed to Peter, James, and John. ESPECIALLY AFTER PETER SUGGESTED MAKING THREE TABERNACLES (one for Jesus, Moses, and Elijah), THE VOICE REDIRECTS ATTENTION NOT TO MOSES, NOT TO ELIJAH, BUT TO JESUS. God sometimes chooses external manifestations (voice, dove, cloud, fire, talking donkeys), not because of multiple divine persons, but because God often reveals Himself through visible/audible signs (burning bush, Sinai thunder and cloud, pillar of fire, voice from heaven, dove descending at baptism, etc). These are manifestations of the one God communicating with humans; public revelation, not conversations between multiple divine persons.

6.x: “sore afraid”: the disciples are afraid of YHWH’s voice affirming the unique supremacy of Jesus over Moses and Elijah. This mirrors the classic OT response whenever YHWH manifests Himself in glory. At Sinai, Israel feared hearing God’s voice directly (Ex 20:18-19). If God had remained only as the consuming fire of Sinai, fallen humans would only recoil. But God desired more than terror-filled worship. He desired fellowship, sonship, and love. So “the Word was made flesh, and dwelt(tabernacled) among us…” (Jn 1:14 KJV). He came in a form we could hear, touch, eat with, walk with, embrace, instead of only thunder, fire, cloud, and trembling. He made it easier for us to genuinely love Him by coming in as the most just, humble, innocent person in history, yet victim to the evilness of this world. Loving Jesus is easy. Loving an overwhelming thunderous voice from heaven is not.

7.x: This action highlights Jesus’ role as the mediator between humanity and the overwhelming presence of the Father. The physical touch breaks their paralysis. “For there is ONE(heis: singular masculine one that demands one person) God, and one mediator between God and men, the MAN(not another God) Christ Jesus” (1 Tim 2:5 KJV). The man Jesus, as a mediator, needs to be a sinless human in order to connect us to the divine Spirit. A God cannot mediate between God and humans, only a sinless man can. Right now, glorified Jesus is sitting on the throne of God. The work is done. The sacrifice is done. Jesus is not interceding for us before the Father continually offering sacrifices every time we sin. Rather, Jesus, as glorified human flesh in heaven sitting on the throne of God, by simply being there intercedes for us the same way the blood of the lamb interceded for the Jews during Passover. There is only one on the throne (Rev 4:8), and this one is described as: (1) God (invisible divine Spirit), and (2) the lamb (the visible glorified flesh of the man Jesus) UNDER ONE FACE and UNDER ONE NAME (Rev 22:3-4). However, this human person, this mediatorial role is temporary, it will end when the Son submits himself to the Father: "And when all things shall be subdued unto him, then shall the Son also himself be subject unto him that put all things under him, that God may be all in all." (1 Cor 15:28). How does God manage to play both King and Prince, God and human, first and last, root & descendant? Well, that’s definitely the mystery: “And without controversy great is the mystery of godliness: God was manifest in the flesh, justified in the Spirit, seen of angels, preached unto the Gentiles, believed on in the world, received up into glory.” (1 Tim 3:16 KJV). Notice the mystery IS NOT how a Trinity works, but how the one God manifested Himself in flesh: “Now a mediator is not a mediator of one, but God is one(heis: singular masculine one that demands one person/subject).”

The Amplified version is a literal translation that amplifies the Greek to give you more than one Greek translation. It also makes more explicit what the Greek demands. “Heis” is the singular masculine noun in Greek used for God, showing that God chose to disclose Himself as a single masculine person/subject, that’s why the Amplified Bible rendered Gal 3:20 as: “Now a go-between (intermediary) has to do with and implies more than one party [there can be no mediator with just one person]. Yet God is [only] ONE PERSON” (AMPC). Trinitarians usually teach that God is “echad”(Hebrew word for “one” that could imply a unity). They cite Deut 6:4: “The LORD our God is one(echad) LORD” (KJV), and then argue that “echad” allows for a plurality of persons within the Oneness of God. While that is true (that the Hebrew “echad” could imply a unity, just like “one” in English and “uno” in Spanish), what they don’t tell you is that Jesus himself cites Deut 6:4 in Mark 12:29. However, the NT was written in Greek, so the excuse used for “echad” no longer works in Mark, because Jesus used “heis” for “one” in Greek, meaning a singular masculine one that demands one person/subject. If God was a plurality of persons, then it’d use “hen,” which is the neuter form of “one” in Greek. You can see an example of this in John 10:30: "I and my Father are one(hen: neuter form of one since it acts as a unity)" - here you find the unity of the human Jesus & the divine Spirit of the Father, the two witnesses of Jesus: “I am one that bear witness of myself, and the Father that sent me beareth witness of me” (Jn 8:18 KJV). “Mia” is used for a singular feminine person/subject. For example: “the two shall become one(mia) flesh(a feminine singular word)” (Eph 5:31 KJV). Hence, the Oneness of God refers to the single divine person that is a Spirit, YHWH, who self identifies as a “He”, not a “they.” Oneness does not teach that the Father(YHWH) is the Son, rather that the Father(YHWH) IS IN the Son (YHWH IS IN the authentic human being born of Mary: “God was IN Christ reconciling the world unto Himself” (2 Cor 5:19 KJV).

8.x: Reassured by Jesus’ touch and voice, the three disciples look up to find that the heavenly vision has concluded. The cloud, the blinding radiance, and the supernatural visitors have vanished. The disappearance of Moses (the Lawgiver) and Elijah (the Prophet) signals that their preparatory roles are complete. They have handed over their administrative and prophetic witness to Jesus. The disciples are left with “Jesus only.” He does not share the stage, the authority, or the tabernacles with anyone else. The Law and the Prophets have receded into the background, leaving Christ as the solitary, supreme authority whom the Father explicitly commanded them to “hear.” Whatever Jesus says is the Word of the Father Himself: “For I have not spoken of myself; but the Father which sent me, he gave me a commandment, what I should say, and what I should speak. And I know that his commandment is life everlasting: whatsoever I speak therefore, even as the Father said unto me, so I speak.” (Jn 12:49-50 KJV) & “the words that I speak unto you I speak not of myself: but the Father that dwelleth in me, he doeth the works.” (Jn 14:10 KJV).

9.x: The visionary preview of the kingdom’s glory is over, and the group must return to the plain of everyday ministry, conflict, and the path to the cross. The glor on the mountain was meant to fortify the disciples for the descent, not replace it. “Tell the vision to no man”: Jesus keeps reminding them of the Messianic Secret. If they were to broadcast what they had just seen, it would fuel popular, nationalistic, and militaristic expectations of a conquering Messiah, completely undermining his immediate mission. “Until the Son of man be risen again”: Jesus sets a definitive legal expiration date on this order of secrecy. The Transfiguration cannot be properly understood apart from the Resurrection. If the disciples preached a glorified Jesus without the context of his sacrificial death and resurrection, they would be preaching a crown without a cross, the very mistake Peter made in Mt 16:23. Once Jesus has been executed and raised from the dead, the puzzle pieces would lock into place. At that point, the testimony of these three eyewitnesses would serve as foundational legal evidence for the authority of the early ekklesia (assembly of believers/church) and the true nature of Christ’s heavenly kingdom.

10.x: Following the command to keep the Transfiguration a secret until after the Resurrection, the disciples are left with a pressing theological dilemma. They have just seen Elijah on the mountain, but Jewish tradition (grounded in Scripture) stated that Elijah had to arrive before the Messiah established his kingdom: "Behold, I will send you Elijah the prophet before the coming of the great and dreadful day of the LORD." (Mal 4:5 KJV). The disciples had just seen Elijah, so if Elijah’s public ministry is supposed to pave the way for the kingdom, why is Jesus acting in reverse order, preaching the kingdom and keeping Elijah a secret? They are trying to reconcile official scribal eschatology with what they just witnessed.

11.x: Jesus validates the textual interpretation of the scribes and confirms Malachi’s prophecy; the arrival of a precursor figure is a strict chronological prerequisite in God’s administrative timeline. “Restore all things”: The Greek word for “restore” is apokatastesei, meaning to reconstitute, reform, or set things back in their proper legal and moral order. Elijah’s ultimate prophetic mission was to call Israel back to covenant fidelity, turning the hearts of the fathers to the children (Mal 4:6) to prepare the nation’s heart for the arrival of its King (the same YHWH of the OT in the flesh).

12.x: Jesus surprises the disciples. The prophecy has already been fulfilled, but not in the literalistic manner the scribes anticipated. The “Elijah” figure did not drop out of heaven in a fiery chariot; he had already walked the earth. “They knew him not”: The religious and political authorities failed to recognize his true spiritual identity, office, and legal authority. They misread the signs of the times. “But have done unto him whatsoever they listed”: “listed” means desired or wished. Instead of repenting at his preaching, the ruling powers treated him with contempt. Specifically, King Herod Antipas imprisoned and ultimately beheaded him to satisfy a personal and political grudge (Mt 14:1-12). “Likewise shall also the Son of man suffer of them”: The rejection of the herald mirrors the rejection of the King. If the authorities ruthlessly executed the “Elijah” of Malachi 4, they will do the exact same thing to the Son of Man. Jesus uses this discussion to shatter any remaining delusions the disciples have about an immediate, painless, military takeover of Jerusalem. The path to the glory they saw on the mountain runs directly through suffering and execution.

13.x: The puzzle pieces finally click into place for Peter, James, and John. Jesus’ explanation shifts their perspective form a literalistic expectation of a resurrected OT prophet to a spiritual fulfillment. “John the Baptist”: John fulfilled the office of Elijah because he operated “in the spirit and power of Elias” (Lk 1:17 KJV), preaching radical repentance, wearing the same distinct hairy garment and leather belt (2 Kings 1:8; Mt 3:4), and confronting corrupt rulers. By identifying John as the martyred Elijah, Jesus ensures the disciples realize that the countdown to his own crucifixion has officially entered its final phase.

14.x: This marks the sharp transition from the quiet isolation of the mountain to the chaotic, demanding reality of human need. While Peter wanted to stay on the mountain in permanent tents, the real mission requires descending into the crowd. Marks’ account adds that a crowd had gathered around the remaining nine disciples, and the scribes were actively arguing with them over their failure (Mk 9:14).

15.x: The man bypassed the disciples, who have failed him, and takes his case directly to the ultimate authority. He begins to ask for mercy, recognizing that he has no right to demand a cure. The KJV uses the term “lunatick”, which translates the Greek verb selēniazetai, literally meaning “moon-struck.” In 1st-century vernacular, this term described the physical manifestations of what we recognize today as epilepsy (seizures, foaming at the mouth, rigidity). “Ofttimes he falleth into the fire, and oft into the water”: The spirit is actively attempting to destroy the boy’s life by driving him into lethal environments (burning him or drowning him). This highlights the malicious intent of the spiritual forces that try to destroy their host. We see an example of this when Jesus sends a legion of demons into a herd of pigs, and they immediately jump off the cliff and self-destroy (Mt 8:32).

16.x: In Mt 10:1, Jesus had explicitly called his twelve disciples together and "gave them power against unclean spirits, to cast them out, and to heal all manner of sickness and all manner of disease.” However, despite having been granted this authority earlier, the nine disciples suffered a catastrophic administrative and spiritual failure in the valley while Jesus was on the mountain. Why did the delegated authority of the apostles fail against this specific affliction? It reveals that authority is not an automatic, mechanical magic trick, but something that requires active spiritual alignment, which the disciples had let slip in Jesus’ physical absence.

17.x: Following the disciples’ failure to cast out the demon (the nine without Peter, James, and John), Jesus reacts with sharp frustration, and uses language reminiscent of Moses’ indictment of Israel in Deuteronomy 32:5 (“they are a perverse and crooked generation”) and Deuteronomy 32:20 (“a very froward generation, children in whom is no faith”). This rebuke includes the disciples themselves as “faithless” and “perverse”, which means “turned aside”, “distorded”, or “warped from the correct spiritual path.” Despite seeing miracles for years, they still default to spiritual impotence. “How long shall I suffer you”: “Suffer” here means to bear with, endure, or tolerate. This is a rare, raw glimpse into Christ’s internal weight. Knowing that his crucifixion is fast approaching, he expresses profound grief that his closest followers are still entirely unequipped to carry on the administration of the kingdom without his physical presence.

18.x: Jesus does not perform a medical procedure or an elaborate, drawn-out ritual; he issues a decisive judicial command (rebuked). The demonic entity has no legal standing or power to resist the direct verbal command of Christ. It immediately vacates the premises. The cure is instantaneous and permanent. They physical symptoms vanish the exact moment the underlying spiritual oppression is evicted.

19.x: Embarrassed by their highly public failure in front of the multitudes and the scribes, the disciples wait until they are in private (“apart”) to conduct a debrief. “Why could not we cast him out?”: They remember that Jesus had given them the authority to cast out unclean spirits (Mt 10:1), and they had successfully done it before (Lk 10:17). They want to know where the system broke down.

20.x: Jesus does not blame the demon for being too strong, nor does he say God withheld His power. He places the failure squarely on the disciples’ unbelief (apistian). They had treated the power delegated to them as an automatic, mechanical ritual rather than maintaining an active, dependent relationship with the Source of that power. “Faith as a grain of mustard seed”: the point is not that they need a massive amount of faith; the point is that even a minuscule of genuine, living faith (faith that is properly anchored in the omnipotence of God rather than human effort) holds immense administrative power. Quality over Quantity. “Say unto this mountain, remove hence to yonder place”: Moving mountains was a common Jewish hyperbole used to describe overcoming seemingly impossible, insurmountable difficulties (great rabbis who could resolve massive legal dilemmas were often called “rooters up of mountains”). “Nothing shall be impossible unto you”: When a representative of the King is operating in perfect, unbroken faith and alignment with the King’s legislative will, the entire backing of the heavenly courts is at their disposal.

21.x: You can only find this verse in Bibles based on either the TR or the MT (KJV, NKJV, Reina-Valera, MEV, WEB, etc). If you open a modern translation like the ESV, NIV, or NASB based on the CT, you will notice that this verse is either entirely missing from the main text (jumping from verse 20 straight to 22) or place inside brackets with a footnote. 87.7% of Greek manuscripts contain this verse, however, the oldest 2 manuscripts (0.6%) do not have it (percentages come from The Text-Critical English New Testament Byzantine Text Version by Robert Adam Boyd), so many Scholars choose to follow the oldest manuscripts even though they are the minority. Theologically, this verse provides the final, vital piece of instruction to the disciples regarding their spiritual power failure with the demonic boy. In v. 20, Jesus told them they failed because of their “little faith” and explained the power of a mustard seed of faith. Verse 21 adds a crucial operational nuance: spiritual preparation. Jesus indicates that certain intense types (“this kind”) of spiritual oppression cannot be overcome by a generic invocation of authority or a mechanical ritual. They require an active, deeply disciplined lifestyle of self-denial (fasting) and direct communion with God (prayer). It teaches that power in the valley is directly proportional to devotion in secret. I believe it is an error of the modern CT to remove this verse. First, because it does have a parallel passage, which indicates that this is not new information: “This kind can come forth by nothing, but by prayer and fasting” (Mk 9:29 KJV). 99.7% of Greek manuscripts read like that in Mark. The oldest two manuscripts (0.2%) almost read identical, but are missing the “fasting” part. In a version based on the CT like the Berean Standard Bible, it reads: “This kind cannot come out, except by prayer.” (Mk 9:29 BSB). So the question is, does fasting help? I believe “fasting” does belong there because: (1) Overwhelming numerical and majority of surviving Greek manuscripts do contain it. Its inclusion means trusting the massive, collective, consensus of the historical church’s copying lineage rather than relying exclusively on a tiny handful of isolated Alexandrian (Egyptian) manuscripts that were never copied due to quality issues. (2) Massive geographic and early translation spread: long before the 4th-century manuscripts (Sinaiticus and Vaticanus, which are the foundation of the CT text) were written, Matthew 17:21 was already present in ancient translations scattered across the world. It is found in: The Old Latin (Codex Vercellensis & Veronensis): Dating to the 300s, proving it was in circulation in the West early on. The Latin Vulgate (405AC): Jerome, who had access to older manuscripts than we do today, explicitly chose to retain the verse. The Old Syriac and the Peshitta (200-350AC): Proving its deep roots in the Eastern, Syrian church. For the verse to be an accidental addition, scribes across completely different continents and languages would have had to make the exact same “error” at the exact same location independently, which is highly improbable. (3) Several Church Fathers quoted or directly alluded to this verse long before the oldest surviving “omitting” manuscripts were even produced. For example: Clement of Alexandria (200AC) mentions the Savior declaring to the apostles that “such things are accomplished successfully through prayer” in the case of the demoniac. Tertullian (200AC) wrote about using fasting to fight against the “more fierce demons.” Origen (~220AC) explicitly references the wording in his Commentary on Matthew. This historical trail proves the verse was recognized as authentic scripture in the 2nd and 3rd centuries. (4) The more likely scenario is a Scribal Error of Omission. Hand copyists were actually highly prone to accidental omission via a visual slip called homoioteleuton (similar line endings). A tired scribe looking back and forth from his master scroll could easily drop his eyes from the end of verse 20 to the beginning of verse 22, skipping verse 21 entirely. Once that single, flawed master copy was circulated in Egypt, it duplicated the error across that specific Alexandrian(city of Egypt) geographic branch. (5) Perfect contextual harmony & thematic consistency support its inclusion. Matthew’s gospel is uniquely structured as a didactic manual (a teaching gospel). Leaving the passage at verse 20 leaves the lesson on a purely abstract note about “mustard seed faith.” Verse 21 perfectly rounds out the instructional triad of Matthew’s theology: combining faith with practical covenant disciplines (prayer and fasting), matching his instructions given earlier in the Sermon on the Mount (Mt 6).

22.x: Jesus predicts his death and resurrection for a second time in this gospel (the first occurs in Mt 16:21). “Gathering in Galilee”: This marks a transition from the northern region of Caesarea Philippi and the Mount of Transfiguration back into Galilee, Jesus’ primary base of ministry, as they begin the long, final journey toward Jerusalem. “The Son of Man”: this title refers to the eschatological and messianic imagery of Daniel 7, where the Son of Man is given everlasting dominion. The paradox here is profound: the one destined for cosmic authority is about to suffer absolute subjugation. “Is about to be delivered”: this passive construction implies that God is the ultimate agent who hands His human Son over for the redemption of humanity: “He that spared not his own Son, but delivered him up for us all, how shall he not with him also freely give us all things?” (Rom 8:32 KJV).

23.x: “they shall kill him”: The Son of God literally dies on the cross. A God cannot die. The human Jesus is the image of the one true God who is an invisible Spirit. The sinless human is the LAMB OF GOD, NOT GOD-THE-LAMB. Jesus is the vessel and perfect instrument of redemption of the Father. Unlike the first Adam, this second Adam was obedient unto death. However, the human without the divine Spirit is useless: “I can of mine own self do nothing: as I hear, I judge: and my judgment is just; because I seek not mine own will, but the will of the Father which hath sent me.” (Jn 5:30 KJV); “Verily, verily, I say unto you, The Son can do nothing of himself, but what he seeth the Father do…” (Jn 5:19 KJV); “...I do nothing of myself; but as my Father hath taught me, I speak these things.” (Jn 8:28 KJV); “...the Father that dwelleth in me, he doeth the works.” (Jn 14:10 KJV). The Father does not have bones and flesh, so He made Himself a body in which to dwell (Col 2:9; 2 Cor 5:19); and He chose Jesus to be the one person through whom He could enter into our realm in order to let us know about the other Spiritual realm that we were unaware of. When we worship Jesus, we are worshipping the Father Himself, for Jesus is simply His visible image: “Jesus saith unto him, Have I been so long time with you, and yet hast thou not known me, Philip? he that hath seen me hath seen the Father; and how sayest thou then, Show us the Father?” (Jn 14:9 KJV). “And he will be raised on the third day”: Jesus does not claim that he will raise himself; rather, God the Father (the one true God, Jn 17:3) will vindicate him by raising him from the dead. A good question to ask a Trinitarian is: “WHO RAISES JESUS FROM THE DEAD?” In one part it says Jesus raises his own body: “Destroy this temple, and in three days I(Jesus) will raise it up.” (Jn 2:19 KJV). In another part it says it’s the Father: “God the Father, who raised him from the dead." (Gal 1:1 KJV). Yet in another part it says it was the Spirit: “being put to death in the flesh but made alive by the Spirit” (1 Peter 3:18 KJV). A Trinitarian will try to say something like: The Father Wills and initiates the vindication of His Son. The Son actively exercises his divine authority over death to take his life back. And the Spirit acts as the immediate, life-giving power that reanimates Christ’s physical flesh. However, that sounds like mental gymnastics to avoid the fact that they’re all the same divine Spirit who is God. The Bible specifically says that “God is Spirit” (Jn 4:24), and that there is only “one Spirit” (Eph 4:4). Yet in the Bible we see: (1) “Spirit of the LORD(YHWH)” (Isa 11:2); (2) “Spirit of your Father” (Mt 10:20); (3) “Holy Spirit” (Eph 4:30); (4) “Spirit of Jesus Christ” (Phil 1:19); (5) “Spirit of Christ” (1 Peter 1:11); (6) “Spirit” (Rom 8:16); (7) “Spirit of God” (Gen 1:2); etc. The one Spirit that is God is called many things, but it is THE SAME DIVINE PERSON, it is not multiple persons within the Godhead as Trinitarians think. So when it says that the Father raised Jesus from the dead, it means it was the Holy Spirit that raised up Jesus from the dead, because the Father and Holy Spirit ARE THE SAME DIVINE PERSON. Notice how in Mt 1:20, it was the Holy Spirit the one that CONCEIVED (begot) baby Jesus in Mary’s womb, literally becoming Jesus’ Father. The Father is “Holy” (Jn 4:24) and the Father is “Spirit” (Jn 4:24), hence “Holy Spirit.” Likewise, when it says that Jesus will raise himself up from the dead, He is speaking as God, not the Son. He is speaking as the divine Spirit within Jesus, which is the same thing as the Holy Spirit, and the same as the Father. That is why the man Jesus can be said to be “full of the Holy Spirit” (Lk 4:1 BSB) while saying that the Father dwells in him (Jn 14:10; 2 Cor 5:19), “for in him dwelleth all the fulness of the Godhead bodily” (Col 2:9 KJV). In this way, you can say God raised Jesus from the dead, or you can say it was the Father, or the Spirit, or Jesus himself because they’re ALL THE SAME DIVINE PERSON. Just pay attention when Jesus speaks, because he sometimes speaks as the Son (as the authentic human), and sometimes he speaks as the Father (the only true God who is an omnipresent Spirit). It’s actually easy to identify the difference. When Jesus was born a baby (Lk 2:7); grew mentally, physically, spiritually, and socially (Lk 2:52); was tempted by the devil (Lk 4:2); hungered (Mt 4:2); thirsted (Jn 19:28); grew weary (Jn 4:6); prayed (Lk 22:41); literally died (Mk 15:37); was a sacrifice for sin (Heb 10:10-12); did not know all things (Mk 13:32); had no power (Jn 5:30); was inferior to God (Jn 14:28); was a servant (Phil 2:7-8); etc, it refers to the Son (an authentic human born of Mary). However, when Jesus says he’s eternal (Jn 1:1-2; 8:58); when he never changes (Heb 13:8); when he casts out devils (Mt 12:28); when he’s the bread of life (Jn 6:35); when he miraculously feeds multitudes (Mk 6:38-44); when he gives living water (Jn 4:14); when he gives rest (Mt 11:28); when he calms the storm (Mk 4:39-41); when he answers prayer (Jn 14:14); when he heals the sick (Mt 8:16-17; 1 Pet 2:24); when he raises his own body from the dead (Jn 2:19-21); when he forgive sin (Mk 2:5-7); when he knows all things (Jn 21:17); when he has all power (Mt 28:18; Col 2:10); when he was equal to God - was God (Jn 5:18); when he was King of kings, etc, it refers to the Father, the divine Spirit fully dwelling in the man Jesus. Hence, Jesus sometimes speaks as the Son, and sometimes as the Father, so when he said he would raise his own body, he was speaking as the Father fully dwelling in the man Jesus.

24.x: “when they were come to Capernaum”: Capernaum was Jesus’ Galilean headquarters and Peter’s hometown. “..they that received tribute money came to Peter..” : the tribute money refers to the didrachma (half-shekel) tax. This was not a Roman civil tax, but a religious tax required annually of every adult Jewish male for the upkeep and maintenance of the Temple in Jerusalem (based on Ex 30:13). “...Doth not your master pay tribute?”: The tax collectors approach Peter rather than Jesus, perhaps out of respect or intimidation. Essentially asking: “is your teacher observant of the Law, or does he exempt himself from the temple obligations?”

25.x: “He saith, Yes”: Peter answers impulsively, reassuring them that Jessu does pay the tax, likely to avoid controversy. “...Jesus prevented him..”: The word “prevented” is an archaic word that means “to anticipate”, “to precede, or “to go before.” Before Peter can even bring up the interaction, Jesus speaks first, demonstrating the omniscience of his divine omnipresent Spirit. He already knows what happened outside. “...do the kings of the earth take custom or tribute? Of their own children, or of strangers?”: Kings do not tax their own royal family (children); they levy taxes on the subjects and conquered peoples (strangers).

26.x: “Of strangers”: Peter gives the obvious legal answer: citizens and subjects pay, not the royal heirs. “Then are the children free”: This is the core theological point of the passage. Jesus is the Son of God. The Temple is the house of His Father. Therefore, as the true royal heir, the man Jesus is exempt from paying a tax meant for his Father’s house. By extension, his disciples (as children of the kingdom) are also conceptually free from this obligation.

27.x: “..lest we should offend them..”: Even though Jesus is legally and structurally exempt. He waives his rights. He chooses not to claim exemption because doing so would cause unnecessary scandal, making it look like he despised the Temple or the Law, which would hinder his primary ministry. “..go thou to the sea, and cast an hook..”: Peter was a commercial fisherman who normally used large nets. Here, Jesus tells him to use a single hook: a precise, individual catch. “..take up the fish that first cometh up.. Thou shalt find a piece of money..”: The Greek word used here for the coin is a stater. A stater was worth exactly four drachmas (a full shekel). This was the precise amount needed to cover the half-shelkel tax for exactly two people: Jesus and Peter. This is usually called the miracle of the coin in the fish’s mouth. It is a unique narrative found only in Matthew’s gospel. Jesus proves his divine identity twice in this miracle. First, through his omniscience (knowing Peter’s conversation beforehand). Second, through his sovereignty over creation (commanding a specific fish to bite a specific hook at a specific moment with the exact currency needed). He humbles himself to pay a tax he does not owe, utilizing the natural world to provide exactly what is required.
